Finite Representations of Structured Dependence

Theory, Chapter 7

theory-07-finite-representations.Rmd

The necessity of finite representation

Chapter 6 established that structured dependence belongs at the latent level. Latent values at different units may be related through spatial proximity, grouping, or other structures. This chapter addresses a further question: how is this dependence represented in practice?

The answer is that any practical representation is finite. It involves a finite number of parameters, a finite set of relationships, and a finite specification of how information flows among units. This finiteness determines which dependencies the model can express and which it cannot.

A model’s dependence structure is not an abstract property that exists independently of how it is represented. The representation is the structure. Different finite representations encode different assumptions about the world, even when they are motivated by the same conceptual goal.

Why full joint specification is infeasible

Consider a dataset with nn plots and KK species. The latent layer contains n×Kn \times K values. A fully general joint distribution over these values would require specifying all pairwise dependencies (and potentially higher-order dependencies) among them.

The number of pairwise relationships grows as the square of the number of latent values. For a modest dataset with 500 plots and 20 species, there are 10,000 latent values and roughly 50 million pairwise relationships. Specifying, storing, and manipulating a joint distribution of this size is not practical. The data cannot inform such a large number of dependencies. The parameters would be weakly identified at best, unidentified at worst.

This is not a limitation of current technology. It is a structural feature of high-dimensional dependence. The space of possible joint distributions is vast. Data can only constrain a small portion of it. Any model that appears to specify a rich joint distribution is implicitly making strong assumptions to reduce the effective dimensionality.

Finite representations as modelling commitments

A finite representation of dependence restricts the class of joint distributions under consideration. This restriction is a modelling commitment. It encodes assumptions about which dependencies matter, which can be ignored, and how information propagates among units.

Common forms of restriction include:

Factorisation. The joint distribution is expressed as a product of conditional distributions, each involving only a subset of variables. This reduces the number of parameters but assumes that certain conditional independencies hold.

Low-rank structure. The covariance or precision matrix is constrained to have low rank, or to be expressible in terms of a small number of factors. This assumes that dependence is driven by a limited number of underlying sources.

Locality. Dependence is restricted to units that are “nearby” in some sense (spatially adjacent, temporally proximate, or connected in a graph). Units that are far apart are assumed conditionally independent given intervening units.

Stationarity or exchangeability. The form of dependence is assumed to be the same across the domain. Spatial correlation has the same structure everywhere; group effects are drawn from a common distribution. This reduces the number of unique parameters.

Each of these restrictions is an assumption. None is automatically justified by the structure of the problem. A model that assumes locality when the true process has long-range dependence will fail to capture important structure. A model that assumes stationarity when the process is heterogeneous will impose false uniformity.

What finiteness constrains

A finite representation determines several aspects of the implied probabilistic structure.

Which pairs of units can be dependent. If the representation specifies that only adjacent units are directly connected, then non-adjacent units can only be dependent through chains of intervening units. If the representation uses a fixed set of factors, then units can only be correlated through shared factor loadings.

How strongly pairs can be dependent. The parameterisation determines the range of possible correlations. A representation with few parameters may not be able to express strong dependence between certain pairs, even if such dependence exists in the data.

How dependence varies across the domain. A stationary representation implies the same correlation between any two units at a given distance. A non-stationary representation allows correlation to vary, but requires additional parameters to specify how.

Which conditional independencies hold. The factorisation structure implies specific conditional independencies. These are not tested against the data; they are assumed by construction.

These constraints are necessary. Without constraints, the model would be unidentifiable and uninterpretable. The question is whether the constraints are appropriate for the problem at hand.

The relationship between representation and approximation

It is common to view finite representations as approximations to some “true” infinite or fully general model. This framing can be useful but also misleading.

In some contexts, a well-defined infinite-dimensional object exists (such as a continuous spatial process) and finite representations can be understood as discretisations or truncations of it. This perspective is valuable for understanding limiting behaviour and for connecting finite models to theoretical foundations.

However, the finite representation is what the model actually specifies for inference. The infinite object, if it exists, is a conceptual scaffold. In other contexts (where units are discrete: plots, samples, individuals) there may be no natural infinite-dimensional object to approximate. The dependence structure is whatever the model says it is. The finite representation is the complete specification.

The practical implication is that “approximation” can suggest accuracy improves as the representation becomes richer. This is not always true. A richer representation may introduce more parameters than the data can support, leading to overfitting or identifiability problems. A simpler representation may be more robust and interpretable, even if it deviates from some idealised target. The quality of a representation should be judged by its fit to the problem, not by its proximity to an abstract ideal.

Information flow and its limits

A key consequence of finite representation is that information can only flow through the pathways the representation provides.

Consider a spatial model where dependence is specified through local connections. If two plots are far apart, information about one plot’s latent value can only influence the other through a chain of intermediate plots. If the chain is long, the influence is attenuated. The representation imposes a limit on how far information can travel.

Similarly, consider a factor model where latent values are driven by a small number of shared factors. Information about one unit’s latent value can only inform another’s through the shared factors. If the factors do not capture the relevant variation, the dependence will be missed.

These limits are consequences of the representation. A model that allows information to flow everywhere would be unidentifiable. The representation determines where information flows and where it does not.

Choosing a representation

The choice of finite representation should be guided by:

The structure of the problem. If units are arranged in space, spatial representations are natural. If units fall into groups, hierarchical representations are natural. The representation should reflect the geometry of the problem.

The scale of the data. Richer representations require more data to estimate. A representation that is appropriate for a large dataset may be overparameterised for a small one.

The scientific question. If the goal is to estimate average effects, a simpler representation may suffice. If the goal is to characterise spatial structure, a richer representation is needed.

Identifiability. The representation must be identifiable given the data. If certain parameters cannot be estimated, they should not be included, or their role in the model should be understood as regularisation rather than inference.

There is no universally correct representation. The choice is part of the modelling process. It should be made explicitly and defended on substantive grounds.

Summary

Any practical model of structured dependence uses a finite representation. This representation defines which dependencies the model can express, how information flows among units, and which conditional independencies are assumed.

Finite representations restrict the space of possible joint distributions. These restrictions are modelling commitments. They encode assumptions about locality, stationarity, factorisation, or dimensionality. Different representations imply different models, even when motivated by the same conceptual goal.

The choice of representation should be guided by the structure of the problem, the scale of the data, and the scientific question. It should not be viewed as an approximation to some ideal infinite model. The representation is the model’s specification of dependence.

This chapter establishes that the choice of representation is fundamental, a defining element of the framework rather than a detail to be deferred to implementation.
